title: Stripping and refreshing the wax finish on an oak side table
subtitle: Remove old wax buildup from an oak table surface with white spirit and apply a fresh wax finish
excerpt: How to strip accumulated wax and grime from an antique or vintage oak table surface and restore it with fresh beeswax or carnauba furniture wax. Covers cleaning with white spirit, fine sanding, applying wax in thin coats, and burnishing to a lasting finish.
sourceNotes: Traditional furniture polish practice. Period furniture care manuals (pre-1928 public domain).

glossaryTerms.definition: A traditional wood finish based on natural beeswax dissolved in a solvent (turpentine or white spirit). Applied in thin coats and buffed when dry, beeswax gives a low-sheen, slightly soft finish that feeds and protects the wood. On open-grained timbers like oak, beeswax needs to be re-applied once or twice a year. Not a hard film-forming finish: it does not protect against water rings as effectively as a lacquer or oil finish.

Successive coats of wax polish applied over years without stripping create a soft, opaque yellow layer on the surface that obscures the grain and gathers dust. Wax buildup is removed with white spirit on fine steel wool (0000 grade). The spirit dissolves the wax; the steel wool abrades the softened film without scratching the underlying wood.

is applied. The stripping exposes the original wood colour and grain; the fresh wax nourishes the timber and gives a clean, even finish.

Work in a ventilated room. Apply white spirit liberally to a small section of the table surface with an old cloth or a fine steel wool pad (0000 grade). Rub in the direction of the grain with moderate pressure: the white spirit dissolves the wax and the fine steel wool abrades the softened film. Wipe off the loosened wax with a clean cloth before it can redeposit. Work in sections of about 300 x 300 mm. Allow the white spirit to evaporate fully before moving on (at least 20 minutes per section in a warm room).

Once the whole surface has been stripped and allowed to dry, examine it in raking light for scratches, dents, or uneven colour. Light scratches in the surface wax layer will have been removed by the stripping. Deep scratches that penetrate the wood can be filled with a wax crayon furniture repair stick in a matching colour. Lightly sand the whole surface with 240-grit abrasive paper on the sanding block, working in the direction of the grain. Remove all sanding dust with a clean cloth.

Apply beeswax or carnauba furniture wax in a thin even film using a lint-free cloth, working in the direction of the grain. A thin coat is better than a thick one: a thick coat dries slowly and stays sticky. Allow the first coat to dry until it appears cloudy and matt (typically 30 to 60 minutes). Buff with a clean cloth or a soft shoe brush until the surface is smooth and begins to shine. Apply a second coat in the same way.

Allow the second coat to harden for several hours, then burnish vigorously with a soft cloth or a brush. The friction of burnishing polishes the wax to a low sheen that is characteristic of a wax-finished piece. The sheen deepens with each re-wax over the years.

attrs.cause: Wax applied too thickly and not fully spread before drying.
attrs.fix: Re-apply a thin coat of white spirit to the streaky area to redissolve the wax, wipe off, and re-apply a thinner wax coat.

attrs.symptom: Water marks reappear immediately on the fresh wax
attrs.cause: Wax finish is not a waterproof coating; any liquid left on the surface will leave a ring.
attrs.fix: Fresh water rings in wax can be removed by rubbing with a cloth dipped in a small amount of mayonnaise (emulsion of oil), left for an hour, and polished off. For a table with regular water exposure, consider a hard oil finish instead of wax.
